hints: Remember boiling a simple molecular liquid breaks forces between molecules, not bonds inside molecules, so focus on intermolecular forces.
Both $\text{N}_2$ and $\text{CO}$ have $M_r = 28$ and 14 electrons, so their London dispersion forces are very similar.
Notice $\text{CO}$ is made from two different atoms while $\text{N}_2$ is symmetrical, so think about which one can have extra dipole-dipole attraction and a slightly higher boiling point.
walkthrough:
**Remember what boiling actually breaks**

Boiling separates whole molecules from each other. It overcomes intermolecular forces. It does not break strong covalent bonds inside the molecules.

Rule to remember:
$$\text{boiling point increases as intermolecular attraction increases}$$

**Compare $\text{N}_2$ and $\text{CO}$ fairly**

Both have $M_r = 28$. Both have 14 electrons ($\text{N}_2$: 7 + 7, $\text{CO}$: 6 + 8). So London dispersion forces are almost identical and cannot explain the 5 K difference.

**Spot the key difference in polarity**

$\text{N}_2$ is non-polar and symmetrical, so it has induced dipole-dipole (London) forces only. $\text{CO}$ is heteronuclear with different electronegativities for C and O, so it has a permanent dipole plus London forces.

$$\text{CO: London + permanent dipole-dipole > N}_2\text{: London only}$$

**Link stronger forces to higher boiling point**

The extra permanent dipole-dipole attraction in $\text{CO}$ needs a little more kinetic energy to overcome. That is why $\text{CO}$ boils at 82 K compared to 77 K for $\text{N}_2$.

options.A: Correct. $\text{CO}$ is polar and has permanent dipole-dipole forces in addition to London forces, while non-polar $\text{N}_2$ has London forces only. Stronger total intermolecular attraction gives $\text{CO}$ the higher boiling point.
options.B: Incorrect. Both molecules have $\sigma$ and $\pi$ bonding. $\text{CO}$ is isoelectronic with $\text{N}_2$ and also has a triple bond ($\text{C}\equiv\text{O}$), not $\sigma$ only. This confuses bond type with intermolecular force.
options.C: Incorrect. Boiling does not break the $\text{N}\equiv\text{N}$ or C-O covalent bonds. It only overcomes weak forces between molecules. This is the classic trap of mixing up strong intramolecular bonds with weak intermolecular forces.
options.D: Incorrect. Count the electrons: $\text{N}_2$ has 7 + 7 = 14, $\text{CO}$ has 6 + 8 = 14. They have the same number of electrons, so London forces are very similar and this cannot explain the difference.
